h1: What a head brewer actually does all week, beyond brewing
title: What a Head Brewer Does All Week | Craft Beer School
desc: A realistic week in the life of a head brewer: planning, cellar work, quality, people, paperwork and the small part that is actually brewing.
teaser: Brew day is one day. The other six are spreadsheets, tank juggling, tasting panels and a pump that will not prime.
standfirst: People picture a head brewer stirring a mash tun. The real job is closer to running a small factory that happens to be alive. Here is how the week actually splits up.
sections: The brew is the smallest part

In a typical brewpub or small production brewery, the head brewer might brew two or three times a week. Each brew day takes eight to ten hours from mash in to a cleaned brewhouse. That sounds like most of the week until you list everything else that has to happen for those brews to become beer people pay for.

The honest picture is that a head brewer is a planner, a quality manager, a maintenance coordinator, a trainer and an excise record keeper. Brewing is the skill that earns the title. Running the rest of the week is what keeps the title.

Most weeks start with the tank plan. Every fermenter and bright tank is booked: which beer is in it, when it reaches terminal gravity, when it will be crashed, when it moves to a bright tank and when it gets packaged or kegged. A sales spike for one beer over the weekend can push the whole schedule.

The head brewer checks the weekend numbers, reorders the brew sequence if needed and confirms that malt, hops, yeast and CO2 are on hand for the week. Running out of a specialty malt on a Wednesday is a planning failure, not bad luck. With imported hops and malt, lead times can run to weeks, so the ordering horizon is longer than people expect.

Every morning, somewhere between 7 and 9, the head brewer or the assistant walks the cellar. Gravity and temperature readings on every fermenting tank, a smell and a taste where it matters, pressure on the bright tanks and a look at the glycol chiller. A lager sitting at 10 °C that should be at 12 °C will finish late. A fermenter that has stopped two points above its usual final gravity needs a decision today.

This round is where most problems get caught early. If you want to see what those readings look like over a fermentation, our guide to reading a fermentation curve walks through it.

Before any beer goes to a tap or a can, someone signs it off. In a small brewery that someone is usually the head brewer. That means checking final gravity, carbonation, clarity and taste against the brand standard. It also means holding a batch back when it is not right. Holding a batch costs tank space and sales. Releasing a faulty one costs reputation.

Many head brewers run a short tasting panel once or twice a week with the team, using a shared vocabulary for faults like diacetyl or oxidation. Our guide to off flavours is a good place to build that vocabulary.
People, cleaning and the things that break

Head brewers manage people. That means rotas, training a new assistant on CIP, checking that cleaning chemical concentrations are right and making sure nobody enters a fermenter without the confined space procedure. Safety and cleaning take more hours each week than recipe design does.

Then there is maintenance. Pump seals wear, gaskets perish, solenoid valves stick and the chiller always picks the hottest week of May to struggle. The head brewer does not fix everything personally, but they need to know enough to diagnose, call the right technician and keep a preventive maintenance list.
Paperwork, excise and the front of house

In India every litre of beer is accounted for. Brew logs, production registers and excise records have to match. The format and frequency depend on the state. A missed entry is a compliance problem, so the head brewer is often the person who reconciles the numbers at the end of each day or week.

In a brewpub there is also the front of house. Staff need to know how to describe the new seasonal. The owner wants to know why the stout costs more to make. Customers ask to meet the brewer. Communication is part of the job.
What this means if you want the job

If you are thinking about becoming a brewer, take two lessons from this. First, the technical base has to be solid, because every decision in that cellar round depends on understanding fermentation, yeast and process. Second, the career is as much about organisation as about creativity. The brewers who move up fastest are the ones who can plan a tank schedule and keep a clean log.

Most people start as an assistant brewer. Our guide to becoming a brewer in India covers the route in.
faqs: How many hours does a head brewer work?
It varies a lot by brewery size, but long days are common, especially on brew days and when a tank or chiller misbehaves. Weekend tastings and events add to it in brewpubs.
Does a head brewer need a degree?
Not always. Many head brewers come up through assistant roles with short courses and certifications. A science background helps with the quality and troubleshooting side of the job.
What is the difference between a head brewer and a brewmaster?
The titles overlap and different breweries use them differently. In larger companies a brewmaster often oversees several brewers or sites, while a head brewer runs one brewhouse day to day.
